Species of the genus Obduodon were the first known premodern taxa of the platypus family Ornithorhynchidae. Two species are currently described, the late Oligocene Obduodon insignis Woodburne and Tedford, 1975, from the Etadunna and Namba formations in central Australia, and the early to middle Miocene Obduodon dicksoni Archer, Jenkins, Hand, Murray, and Godthelp, 1992, from the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in Queensland. Until now, all ornithorhynchid material recovered from Riversleigh, despite variation in size (Archer et al., 1992; Musser and Archer, 1998), has been referred to Ob. dicksoni.
...
Also included within Ornithorhynchidae are the Paleocene Monotrematum sudamericanum Pascual, Archer, Ortiz Jaureguizar, Prado, Godthelp, and Hand, 1992, from Argentina, and the extant modern platypus, Ornithorhynchus anatinus Shaw, 1799, from Australia. Although initially included in Ornithorhynchidae, the Early Cretaceous Stenopodon galmani Archer, Ritchie, Flannery, and Molnar, 1985, from Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, was later placed in the monotypic family Steropodontidae (Flannery et al., 1995). The oldest known monotreme, Teinolophos trusleri Rich, Vickers- Rich, Constantine, Flannery, Kool, and van Klaveren, 1999, was provisionally referred by Rich et al. (2001) to Steropodontidae. Rowe et al. (2008) concluded in contrast that it should be referred to Ornithorhynchidae. Phillips et al. (2009), after reanalyzing previously published data, concluded that it was  

instead a stem monotreme rather than a member of any previously defined family.  

Recent discovery of a morphologically distinctive and very large platypus first lower molar from Two Trees Site at Riversleigh has resulted in recognition of a third, relatively derived species of Obduodon. results.title: Platypus
results.snippet:
The common name "platypus" means "flat- foot", deriving from the Greek word platúpos (πλατύπος), [14] from platús (πλατύς 'broad, wide, flat')[15][a] and poús (πούς 'foot'). [16][17] Shaw initially assigned the species the Linnaean name Platypus anatinus when he described it,[12][10] but the genus term was quickly discovered to already be in use as the name of a beetle genus Platypus.[10] It was independently described as Ornithorhynchus paradoxus by Johann Blumenbach in 1800 (from a specimen given to him by Sir Joseph Banks)[18] and following the rules of priority of nomenclature, it was later officially recognised as Ornithorhynchus anatinus.[19]
...
The scientific name Ornithorhynchus anatinus literally means 'duck-like bird-snout',[12] deriving its genus name from the Greek root ornith- (opvθ ornith or opvics ornis bird')[22] and the word rhúnkhos (puyxos 'snout', 'beak').[23] Its species name is derived from Latin anatinus ('duck-like') from anas 'duck'. [12][24] The platypus is the sole living representative or monotypic taxon of its family (Ornithorhynchidae).[25]

results.snippet:
Species of the genus Obduodon were the first known premodern taxa of the platypus family Ornithorhynchidae. Two species are currently described, the late Oligocene Obduodon insignis Woodburne and Tedford, 1975, from the Etadunna and Namba formations in central Australia, and the early to middle Miocene Obduodon dicksoni Archer, Jenkins, Hand, Murray, and Godthelp, 1992, from the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in Queensland. Until now, all ornithorhynchid material recovered from Riversleigh, despite variation in size (Archer et al., 1992; Musser and Archer, 1998), has been referred to Ob. dicksoni. This material has been collected from Faunal Zone B sites (interpreted to be early Miocene in age; Arena, 2004), including Neville's Garden, Dirk's Towers, and Price is Right sites, and Faunal Zone C sites (interpreted to be middle Miocene; Arena, 2004), including Ringtail (which produced the holotype, a near complete skull), Quentin's Quarry, Bob's Boulders, and Cleft of Ages sites (Archer et al., 1992; Archer et al., 1993; Musser and Archer, 1998). Also included within Ornithorhynchidae are the Paleocene Monotrematum sudamericanum Pascual, Archer, Ortiz Jaureguizar, Prado, Godthelp, and Hand, 1992, from Argentina, and the extant modern platypus, Ornithorhynchus anatinus Shaw, 1799, from Australia. Although initially included in Ornithorhynchidae, the Early Cretaceous Stenopodon galmani Archer, Ritchie, Flannery, and Molnar, 1985, from Lightning Ridge, New South Wales, was later placed in the monotypic family Steropodontidae (Flannery et al., 1995). The oldest known monotreme, Teinolophos trusleri Rich, Vickers- Rich, Constantine, Flannery, Kool, and van Klaveren, 1999, was provisionally referred by Rich et al. (2001) to Steropodontidae. Rowe et al. (2008) concluded in contrast that it should be referred to Ornithorhynchidae. Phillips et al. (2009), after reanalyzing previously published data, concluded that it was  

instead a stem monotreme rather than a member of any previously defined family.  

Recent discovery of a morphologically distinctive and very large platypus first lower molar from Two Trees Site at Riversleigh has resulted in recognition of a third, relatively derived species of Obduodon. Although the Two Trees Local Fauna (LF) was initially regarded as middle Miocene in age (Flannery and Archer, 1987), in part because of its stratigraphic position on the Gag Plateau, Archer et al. (1997) and Scanlon et al. (2003) have suggested that this assemblage may be younger than middle Miocene. Stratigraphic understanding of the Riversleigh local faunas follows Archer et al. (1997), Creaser (1997), and Arena (2004).

It derived from the South Prospect B Site on Lake Namba, from the Namba Formation, in the Callabonna Sub- basin of the Lake Eyre Basin (Woodburne and Tedford 1975). As the result of extensive quarrying at the type locality, Archer et al. (1978) later reported a left dentary fragment preserving the alveoli for m3, m2, and the posterobuccal alveolus for m1 (QM F9558) and a partial left ilium from Queensland Museum, Brisbane, Queensland (QM F9559) that they referred to O. insignis. More recently, Case et al. (2023) briefly described a left upper molar (M1), South Australian Museum, Adelaide, South Australia (SAMA)

P24262, from Mammalon Hill, Ngama Local Fauna (LF), of the upper Oligocene Etadunna Formation, which is the same size and morphology as the holotype of O. insignis and occludes well with that tooth and so was also referred to this species. Formal publication of this specimen is in preparation (J. Case, pers.
...
To date, these are the only published descriptions of remains of monotremes from the Lake Eyre Basin in central Australia. However, Musser (1999) published an abstract in a booklet for the 1999 Annual General Meeting of the Australian Mammal Society where the name Obdurodon griffithsi Musser, 1999 for two molars from Mammalon Hill, Etadunna Formation, central Australia was erected. This name meets ICZN Article 11 (ICZN [International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature] 1999) requirements for availability by publication; meets Article 13.1.1 [... be accompanied by a description or definition that states in words characters that are purported to differentiate the taxon.] in stating 'however, the two molars of Ob. griffithsi differ in number and structure of buccal cuspides and in root number' although it is inadequate to associate the name with a specimen and unclear as to whether the two teeth vary in the stated features, rather than them varying from those of named taxa; and because it was published in 1999, rather than after 1999, Article 16.4.1 [the requirement for explicit fixation of a holotype and intent to deposit it in a collection] does not apply. Musser (1999) mentioned the presence of two molars without giving any indication as to what collection they were in or who collected them. Furthermore, Musser (1999) did not fix a name-bearing type in terms of ICZN Article 72.2, and neither has one been subsequently fixed. Thus, this name may be available in terms of nomenclature, but in the absence of either an illustration or catalogue number for the specimens having been published with the name, it is a nomen dubium and is therefore, not indicative of any taxon and does not increase the diversity of the genus Obdurodon.  

Otherwise, the fossil record of platypuses from Oligocene- Miocene sediments in Australia is informed by discoveries in sites in the Riversleigh World Heritage Area in north- west Queensland. Another ancient platypus Obdurodon dicksoni Archer, Jenkins, Hand, Murray and Godthelp, 1992 was described from a near- complete skull (QM F20568), and 17 teeth and two dentary fragments from Ringtail Site, Ray's Amphitheatre, Gag Plateau, Riversleigh Station and three other sites in Riversleigh Faunal Zones B and C (Archer et al. 1992, 1993). Subsequently, the most recently described fossil species of ancient platypus, Obdurodon tharalkooschild Pain, Archer and Hand, 2013, was based on a single left m1, QM F56252, from Two Trees Site, Gag Plateau, Riversleigh World Heritage Area and is considered Middle Miocene in age (Faunal Zone C) (Pian et al. 2013). Sites from Riversleigh's Faunal Zones B and C have been radiometrically dated to the Early (18.2- 16.5 Ma) and Middle (15.1- 13.5 Ma) Miocene, respectively (Woodhead et al. 2016).  

The general paucity of ornithorhynchid fossils means that the recent discovery of new material attributable to Obdurodon from central Australia is noteworthy. This is described below.
